summary: This document describes the current requirements and requests for enhancements to the format of the canonical version of RFCs. It defines terms to clarify which stages of document production are being discussed. The requirements will guide later format changes. It updates RFC 2223.

plainLanguage.summary: Request for Comments (RFC) 6949 records requirements for the official format of these documents and for producing them. It balances long-term readability with requests for accessibility and more flexible publication formats.

subtitle: Requirements proposed in 2013 for the canonical format and publication of RFCs.

tldr.problem: The established RFC format had strict text and page limits, while readers and authors requested richer diagrams, more characters, and reflowable text.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines document-format terms, reviews arguments about proposed changes, and lists requirements to retain, add, or retire.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 2223 and sets requirements, leaving detailed implementation rules to later documents.

today: RFC 6949 is Informational and updates RFC 2223. It sets format requirements and leaves detailed implementation rules to later documents.

sections.title: Why Review the RFC Format
sections.content:
The RFC Series adopted a common format to keep documents readable, editable, and archivable as tools changed. Its use of US-ASCII and a stable presentation format helped the series work across devices and editing systems.

As reading devices and display technology changed, authors and readers requested new ways to present RFC content. This RFC records requirements for considering those changes, with a focus on the canonical format.
sections.plainLanguage: A stable format helped RFCs remain readable over time. This document records how the format might adapt while preserving that reliability.

sections.title: The Stages of an RFC Document
sections.content:
The canonical format is the authorized and archived version. The publication format is the version readers see or print. The revisable format is used by the RFC Editor to create publication formats, and the submission format is what authors send to the editor.

The RFC also defines reflowable text as text that wraps when a reader changes the window or font size. Metadata is information describing a document's structure or elements, such as its topic or author.
sections.plainLanguage: An RFC moves from an author's submission through editing to an official archived copy and reader-facing copies. The RFC gives each stage a separate name.

sections.title: Arguments for and against Change
sections.content:
The RFC summarizes arguments for and against changing ASCII diagrams, character encoding, pagination, reflowable text, and metadata. Plain text can be easy to search and preserve, while richer graphics and wider character support can help explain some material and names.

Pages can help readers cite and print documents, while removing fixed pagination may improve reading on different screens. Reflowable text can help on small displays but may affect tables and diagrams. Metadata may make documents easier to use but also adds process and compatibility costs.
sections.plainLanguage: Each proposed change has benefits and costs. The RFC records both sides rather than treating every suggestion as a settled requirement.

sections.title: Requirements for the Series
sections.content:
Four original requirements are retained: published content must not change, the canonical format must remain durable, at least one publication format must be plain text, and structure must follow RFC and style-guide rules. New requirements address accessibility, English and character encoding, metadata, graphics, offline publication, fixed-width code, printing, and machine-readable structure.

The RFC also sets process requirements for revisable formats, submission files, publication formats, and checking tools. It proposes retiring the fixed page limit, maximum line length, and requirement that all text be ASCII. It updates RFC 2223; detailed rules were left to a future RFC and the style guide.
sections.plainLanguage: The requirements preserve stable content and a plain-text option while adding accessibility and tooling goals. They also propose removing fixed page and line limits.
